subject: Cooking
title: Garam Masala: India's Warming Blend
description: A 60-second lesson on Garam Masala: India's Warming Blend.

hook.text: 'Garam' means 'hot' in Hindi — but garam masala isn't spicy. It's warming, according to Ayurvedic medicine.

buildup.text: The blend typically combines cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, cumin, and coriander — all 'warming' spices.

discovery.text: Every Indian family has their own garam masala recipe, passed down through generations.

twist.text: Pre-made store versions use a standard formula, but authentic garam masala varies by region and household.

climax.text: It's added at the end of cooking — heat releases aroma but prolonged cooking destroys its delicate oils.

punchline.text: Garam masala isn't a recipe. It's a family signature.

quiz.question: When is garam masala traditionally added to a dish?

details.summary: Garam masala is a warming Indian spice blend whose composition varies by region and family. Common ingredients include cumin, coriander, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and black pepper.
details.whyItMatters: Garam masala demonstrates how spice blending creates complexity beyond individual ingredients. Every Indian household has its own recipe, making it deeply personal and culturally significant.
takeaways: Recipes vary widely by region, family, and personal preference
Added near the end of cooking to preserve aromatic compounds
Warming spices like cardamom and cinnamon define its character

faq.question: What is the difference between garam masala and curry powder?
faq.answer: Garam masala is an aromatic finishing blend from Indian tradition. Curry powder was invented by the British to approximate Indian flavors and typically includes turmeric, which garam masala does not. Curry powder is cooked into dishes early; garam masala is added at the end.

faq.question: Should you make your own garam masala?
faq.answer: Freshly toasted and ground whole spices produce dramatically better garam masala than pre-ground store-bought versions. The volatile oils that provide aroma dissipate quickly once ground. Even a simple homemade blend outperforms most commercial options.
